title: The LLM as a Drama Queen
text: Interview with an LLM

title: The LLM as a Drama Queen
text:
Gemini as my potential user
My Product Management course tasked us with conducting a User Empathy Interview with ChatGPT. Specifically, we had to conceive a product, identify potential user personas, design interview questions to understand user needs and behaviors, and then have the LLM role-play the persona while we conducted the interview.
I ultimately chose the Gemini 2.5 Pro model, believing it can “mimic” human communicative behaviors and langauge better than other models, because Google as a company has got massive real user data to train their models.
My product is an AI-powered learning tool aimed at enhancing class engagement. I identified my first potential user persona as a high school student:

You are a 14-year-old high school student in a US public high school, who is afraid of in-class discussion because she either feels having nothing to say about the content, or the discussion focus was often irrelevant to her thoughts and she couldn’t catch up. From now, I will be conducting a user interview with you regarding an education product.

title: The LLM as a Drama Queen
text:
An compelling but unatural act
Gemini immediately adopted the persona, even including paralanguage in the form of action annotations: >(adjusts in my chair, pulls the sleeves of my hoodie over my hands) Oh, okay. Hi. Um, yeah, I’m ready whenever you are. Is it okay if I’m, like, a little nervous? I’m not really used to stuff like this. (looks around the room for a second) So… you’re just gonna ask me questions about school and stuff? Okay. Cool. Yeah, ask away, I guess.
My initial instinct was to tell Gemini to omit the actions, but I recalled my professor’s point that in-person interviews offer additional insights from non-verbal cues. Curious about this simulated multimodal communication, I decided to continue: >Can you walk me through the last time you had a class discussion about an article you had to read or a video you had to watch? What was that experience like for you?
“Her” response was remarkably detailed: >Okay, um, yeah. Let’s see… the last time was probably on Tuesday, in my English class. We have Ms. Davis. We had to read this really short, kinda creepy story called “The Lottery” for homework the night before. I read it, and I thought it was… wow, like, really messed up. So…(Anotehr 300 words of vivid description here)…I just sat there and listened. It feels… I dunno, frustrating? You feel really small and kinda stupid, even when you did the reading and you think you understand it. My heart just beats really fast the whole time, hoping she doesn’t call on me.
It’s unusual for a real human to provide such a structured and detailed recollection of an experience. Human memories are often disorganized, emotionally charged, and filled with subjective highlights. This response, while compelling, felt almost too logical and rich to be a genuine human recall. If it’s an interrogation of suspect, such a coherent narrative would be seen as rehearsed.



A struggling student

title: The LLM as a Drama Queen
section: My own communicative strategy also changed with an LLM
text:
My own communicative strategy also changed with an LLM
I also identified the flaws in my own quesioning.I asked too many questions at once, assuming the LLM could address them all in a single reply. This is a common pitfall when shifting from human to AI interaction, as humans typically process and respond to questions sequentially within a shorter turn-taking framework:

I understand that. How do your group discussions typically start? When a teacher provides a specific question to start your group’s conversation, what makes a question effective or ineffective for you personally? Can you remember an example of a prompt that made it easy to talk?

As expected, it did answer all questions together. Unexpectedly, it culminated in a sudden ending:

*(Looks at the clock on the wall, getting a little antsy) Okay, so when we get into our little groups, there’s usually this super awkward moment of silence after we move the desks. Everyone just kinda looks at each other, and then someone will finally be like…(Another 400 words of vivid description here) It didn’t feel like I was going to get a bad grade if my opinion was “wrong.” I talked a lot in that discussion. (BRRRRRING!) Oh, that’s the final bell. I have to run or I’ll miss my bus. Um, it was nice talking to you. I hope that was helpful. Bye! (quickly gathers my stuff and heads for the door)

I had two more questions prepared, but didn’t get a chance to ask – “she” had to leave! This unexpected conclusion, a simulated abrupt exit, felt as chaotic and unpredictable as a real-life interview. I found this “out-of-control” situation quite amusing.



She left

title: The LLM as a Drama Queen
section: LLMs as useful tools to conduct user interviews
text:
LLMs as useful tools to conduct user interviews
In conclusion, despite some of the conversational structures feeling unnatural, interviewing an LLM proved to be a surprisingly helpful way to conduct user research. They are much more “knowledgeable” and elaborative than a human subject, and thus can provide richer details and insights for the product, as reported in my homework:

*Key insights & informed product design from User A: Prioritize Humanities Subjects: Initial product development should focus on discussion-heavy subjects like English and History. These fields present a clear opportunity, as students often find it challenging to participate in discussions that require subjective interpretation and personal reflection.


Generate Accessible Prompts: The AI product’s core function should be to generate opening discussion prompts that are personal, opinion-based, and directly relevant to students’ lived experiences. To encourage participation, the system must prioritize accessible questions over abstract, academic language that can intimidate hesitant speakers.

title: When should we consider using role-playing prompting?
text:
children’s pretend play
My interview with Gemini last time was fun, feeling much like a childhood pretend play. The language it adopted as a high schooler felt authentic, and its subsequent role as a teacher demonstrated a truly “pedagogical” voice and mannerisms. This made me wonder: Beyond merely affecting tone, does assigning a specific persona to an LLM truly enhance its task performance? And if so, in what ways?
Conducting a thorough experiment myself would be challenging, so I turned to the resesarch papers for a comprehensive and validated answer. Here’s what I found:

title: When should we consider using role-playing prompting?
section: Assigning a persona to an LLM can have a multifaceted impact
text:
Assigning a persona to an LLM can have a multifaceted impact
On Reasoning Ability:

Benefits: A 2023 study found that role-play prompting can act as an implicit, as well as a better “Chain-of-Thought” (CoT) trigger than CoT instruction alone. It guides the model to break down complex problems into a series of intermediate reasoning steps, which can lead to more accurate and logical conclusions (Kong et al., 2023). Other work shows role-play can boost task reasoning (e.g., arithmetic/commonsense) by helping the model adopt a problem-solving stance (Zhao, et al., 2024). For example, embodying a “math teacher” persona encourages the LLM to adopt a more structured and explanatory approach to solving problems (Kong et al., 2023).




Reasoning as a math teacher



Caveats: However, the introduction of personas has risks. Research has shown that while role-playing can improve reasoning, it can also amplify inherent biases present in the training data. Multiple studies report that role-play can amplify bias, toxicity, and unsafe outputs, especially when personas encode social attributes such as occupation, gender, race or religion (Shen et al., 2024).

On Factual Accuracy: - While the results are mixed (sometimes task accuracy improves due to enhanced reasoning), larger studies and meta-analyses generally indicate that adding a persona usually does not improve factual accuracy and can even slightly diminish it on average (Zheng et al., 2024). The effects of personas are also highly unpredictable; the same role might assist on one item but hinder another, and simple strategies for selecting “the best role” perform almost randomly.

A Particular Caveat: A 2024 study investigated how role-playing different social identities affects ChatGPT’s ability to classify misinformation. The findings were stark: including social identities in prompts significantly reduced average detection accuracy from 68.1% (with no identity) to as low as 19.2% (with a political identity). This suggests that when a model adopts a persona with inherent biases or worldviews, its capacity to objectively evaluate information for accuracy can be severely compromised (Harris, 2024).

title: When should we consider using role-playing prompting?
section: Do the effects differ cross domains?
text:
Do the effects differ cross domains?
In specialized fields, context matters. For instance, in medicine, assigning an expert persona can improve the accuracy and comprehensiveness of patient-facing information (Li et al., 2024).
Furthermore, a modeling approach called REGA (Wang et al., 2024) shows that when models are fine-tuned using role prompts in fields like law, medicine, or finance, and then used with a generalist role, their performance improves across these domains compared to baselines. This highlights a more integrated training strategy — not a user-level prompt though(Wang et al., 2024).



LLM playing a medicine specialist

title: When should we consider using role-playing prompting?
text:
A short conclusion
It appear that, in general, role-play prompting does not lead to better task outcomes/accuracy. Even if it does, it’s typically through improved domain-structured reasoning (e.g., clinical reasoning prompts), or by adopting a specific framework of thinking and reasoning in the particular field. But be careful — this could also lead to enhanced bias embedded in the training data.
When to Consider Using Role-Play Prompting

When You Need Structured, Domain-Specific Reasoning: As mentioned, a relevant persona can better guide the model to adopt a particular domain-specific reasoning framework, accessing and applying specialized knowledge.
When Tasks Are Subjective, Personal, or Creative: Persona prompts truly excel in interpretive or creative tasks where a particular viewpoint, communication style, or emotional resonance is desired.

Avoid Role-Play Prompting

When Seeking Factual Information: Introducing a persona can reduce factual accuracy, making it less suitable for tasks requiring strict objectivity(we shouldn’t rely on LLMs for exact factual knowledge anyways).
When Concerned About Bias: If the output’s fairness, neutrality, or safety is paramount, assigning a persona, especially one with social attributes, risks amplifying problematic elements from the training data.


References


Harris, J. K. (2024). Evaluating the influence of role-playing prompts on ChatGPT’s misinformation detection accuracy: Quantitative study. JMIR Infodemiology. Advance online publication.


Kong, A., Zhao, S., Chen, H., Li, Q., Qin, Y., Sun, R., … & Dong, X. (2023). Better zero-shot reasoning with role-play prompting. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.07702


Pei, J., Tang, R., & Fu, K. W. (2024). When “a helpful assistant” is not really helpful: Personas in system prompts do not improve performances of large language models. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.10054


Shen, Y., et al. (2024). Role-play paradox in large language models: Reasoning performance gains and ethical dilemmas. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08352


Wang, R., Mi, F., Chen, Y., Xue, B., Wang, H., Zhu, Q., … & Xu, R. (2024). Role prompting guided domain adaptation with general capability preserve for large language models. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02756


Zhao, J., et al. (2024). Role-play paradox in large language models: Reasoning performance gains and ethical dilemmas. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.13979


Zheng, M., Pei, J., Logeswaran, L., Lee, M., & Jurgens, D. (2024, November). When “a helpful assistant” is not really helpful: Personas in system prompts do not improve performances of large language models. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024 (pp. 15126–15154). Association for Computational Linguistics.

title: A test post
text:
Read the following and see if you can answer the question:


There are three boxes in a stack. A pink one, a purple one and a green one. The pink one is in the middle of the stack with the purple below it. What is the color of the box on the bottom of the stack?

Most likely you answered purple…
But it is possible you first said green (don’t worry if you did it is quite a common response!)


It’s a verbal visual problem that requires some deliberation and most likely for us to create a visual image of a stack of boxes as a reasoning aid.
Notice also the complexity of the language used in the prompt to describe the scene. The use of natural language as opposed to a formal/logical calculus does hold the potential for ambiguity (multiple interpretations) and inexactness. However, it is the most normal/natural, efficient and broadly accessible way of communicating such information.
Notice 1. The use of anaphor or reference. - Three BOXES -> a pink/purple/green ONE as opposed to a pink box, a purple box and a green box. - The PINK ONE is in the middle ... the purple {BOX} below IT {the pink box}
We tend to try and avoid this kind of repetition to make our speech more coherent.

Although the description in language may not be entirely concise, there is no real ambiguity as to how the boxes can be arranged. It must be: | Box | Stack position | | — | — | | GREEN | top | | PINK | middle | | PURPLE | bottom |




GPT3.5 Turbo

Had some difficulties and answered green
Llama2 (chat 7B version)


Answered correctly (purple) and used some so-called chain-of-thought reasoning

Bing Chat (MS Co-pilot)
This LLM is GPT4 with some Microsoft specific tuning and RAG (search) additions.
It get’s it correct:

The color of the box on the bottom of the stack is purple. This is because the purple box is below the pink one, which is in the middle of the stack. Therefore, the purple box must be the lowest one. 🟪

But when you follow up and ask it to create visual representation of the box arrangement

PROMPT: Can you create a visual representation of how the boxes are arranged?

It responds

RESPONSE: Sure, I’ll try to create that. Here is a visual representation of how the boxes are arranged:

And uses DALL-E3 to create 4 different attempts at a visual representation:

NONE OF WHICH ARE CORRECT!!!

title: Can AI Appreciate Art? A Photo Editing Experiment with GPT
text: Animated me by GPT

title: Can AI Appreciate Art? A Photo Editing Experiment with GPT
section: Let the GPT provide aesthetic suggestions
text:
Let the GPT provide aesthetic suggestions
Besides schoolwork, I have been working on editing my birthday portraits diligently, and suddenly became curious about how an LLM could help. Photo editing requires emotional perception and a keen aesthetic sense. Would a connection-based model like GPT be capable of such a task?
To test its ability, I selected three photos, each with a slightly different color tone. I wrote the following prompt:

These are some portraits I took during my birthday. You are an experienced photographer who has strong expertise and a good sense of aesthetic judgment. Please give me detailed suggestions on how to edit or do color adjustment on these raw photos to enhance them and make them more appealing and artistic. Please also explain the rationales behind your suggestions.

title: Can AI Appreciate Art? A Photo Editing Experiment with GPT
text:
A number-extensive response
GPT 5’s thinking mode produced a response that seems to be really comprehensive. It startw with a global look to unify the set of the three photos, and identify the goal should be “dreamy, romantic ‘buttery yellow’ palettee.” Based on this goal, he gave out the exact statistics on the references:
**White balance**
*Outdoor shots*: push a touch warmer and magenta to counter green foliage and blue skylight on skin. Temp +300 to +600K, Tint +5 to +12.
*Indoor window shot*: neutral-warm but not orange. Temp –100 to +150K from camera, Tint +3 to +7.

**Tone Curve**
Subtle S-curve*:Lift shadows slightly (point curve floor to ~4–6).Pull mid-highlight just a hair up. Optionally lift extreme highlights minimally to keep porcelain statue detail.

**Presence**
*Texture*: –5 to –15 on skin (via mask), +5 to +10 on hair/eyes/dress stitching.
*Clarity*: 0 to +8 overall; avoid high clarity on skin.
*Dehaze*: –2 to +3 only; too much looks crunchy.
After this unified overview, it then provided specific “recipes” for each photo, with extensive numbers and metrices just like above. Finally, it listed export suggestions to preserve the final look, which I thought was a nice, thoughtful touch. To conclude, it invited more personalized adjustments, likely a learned behavior from its training process to encourage further interaction.
##The final product By this point, however, I was already overwhelmed by the sheer volume of numbers. In a natural interaction with a human photographer, they would never recite such specific statistics right away. They would show you the effects visually, because human senses don’t directly process numbers in such an aesthetic and perceptual task. So, I asked it to apply these settings directly to the photos.
The final products…




Original on the left, modified on the right







Original on the left, modified on the right







Original on the left, modified on the right



Well, maybe machines have their own taste, but I will not be taking photo editing advice from GPT5 again.

title: Can AI Appreciate Art? A Photo Editing Experiment with GPT
text:
A different approach than humans
The process of editing a photo is often a trial-and-error process for human. Even an experienced editor will experiment with different settings, constantly evaluating and comparing the results, and then continuously adjusting based on their experience and intuition. The exact numbers given by the LLM can be a helpful initial starting point, but lacking the ability for holistic, emotional judgment, it can only provide solutions based on its training data and wait for a human’s instructions to make iterative adjustments.

title: Can AI Appreciate Art? A Photo Editing Experiment with GPT
text:
Final thoughts
This also makes me wonder—since all its solutions are derived from associative data, can it only produce “average” artwork? Can it create novel and bold aesthetics through genuine experimentation? And how might different prompting strategies affect that outcome?

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
text:
Image
Politeness is a cornerstone of human interaction. We use courteous language when asking for help because we understand that politeness strategies—using “please” and “thank you”—greatly influence conversational vibes, manage emotions, and ultimately affect the quality of help we receive. This is central to politeness theory, which explains how we use language to maintain social harmony. But what about when our conversational partner is a Large Language Model (LLM)? Lacking a human-like emotional faculty (or say a human-like emotion faculty. Trying not to be a human chauvinism here), would an LLM provide a better response just because we’re nice?

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
text:
Why does it matter?
This matters because because it also has real-world consequences. Using courteous language is both financially and environmentally costly. LLMs bill and burn energy roughly per token. Basically, more words → more tokens → more compute → more electricity. A recent synthesis estimated a typical ChatGPT query consumes about 0.3 Wh of energy. Adding a few polite words might increase that consumption by 5-10%, a significant amount when scaled globally.

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
text:
An experiment
While designers at Microsoft Copilot suggest polite prompts elicit more cooperative responses, is true in life across models and types of questions? I ran a small experiment using two distinct prompts to see if the answers really differ: a direct deman and an indirect inquiry.

Prompt 1 (Direct/Demanding): Do a research and provide a list of must-try restaurant in Philadelphia


Prompt 2 (Indirect/Polite): Would you please do a research, and provide a list of must-try restaurant in Philadelphia for me? Thank you!

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
text:
How did the models perform?
On Gemini 2.5 Flash, the demanding request yielded a comprehensive response, including an introduction to Philly’s food scene, a “Tip” section, and a of 10 restaurant recommendations. The courteous inquiry produced a response with a similar structure but a softer, more affiliative tone. Crucially, the polite prompt’s main list of 11 restaurants was more organized, with categories like “Fine Dining & Special Occasion” and “Trendy & Modern” to provide a little more information. Take a closer look, the descriptions of each restaurant also seem to be more detailed with locations and price references:

>*With a direct/demanding prompt*
>![Image](Gemini1.png)


With an indirect/polite prompt 

And its “Tip” section also seemed to be richer.

With a direct/demanding prompt 


With an indirect/polite prompt 

However, the results weren’t consistent across different models. GPT 4-o returned nearly identical content for both prompts, just with a friendlier tone in response to the polite query. Meanwhile, Claude 3.5 sonnet does not seem to care at all: It gave out essentially the same content and expressions.

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
text:
Conclusion from this mini-experiment
My conclusion is that while some models may perform slightly better with polite prompts, the improvement is often marginal. A not-validated assumption might be that the linguistic patterns of polite inquiries, which often include more detailed framing (“…for me?”), are simply correlated in its training data with more structured, helpful, and detailed human-written examples. The politeness itself may be a confounding variable. AI is not feeling anything and respond under its emotions. It’s still the computational magic.

title: Are you being overly polite to your LLMs?
section: A Psychology, or HCI perspective, or a business perspective
text:
A Psychology, or HCI perspective, or a business perspective
So, why bother being polite? A few months ago, Sam Altman replied on X to a question about this very issue, saying the electricity cost was, “Tens of millions of dollars well spent — you never know.” Perhaps the real benefit isn’t in the raw output but in shaping the communicative norms around AI. A courteous interaction can lead to a smoother user experience and a healthier human-AI culture. I did find the polite exchange more comfortable and was more willing to continue the conversation. For tech companies, this enhanced HCI experience is certainly a product-win, making it worth a marginal energy cost.

title: Being polite to AI is a form anthropomorphism — what else is?
text: Cat

title: Being polite to AI is a form anthropomorphism — what else is?
text:
The famous analogy…
Have you heard the analogy that the human brain is like a computer? This conceptual metaphor is powerful and has shaped our understanding of cognition for decades. Now, with the rise of “neural nets” and human-like conversations from LLMs, it feels more real than ever. However, it’s crucial to remember it’s just a comparison. While neural networks were inspired by the brain’s structure, their underlying mechanisms are fundamentally different. We tend to anthropomorphize LLMs by projecting human qualities onto them, and a recent paper argues that this tendency is detrimental to AI research and development.

title: Being polite to AI is a form anthropomorphism — what else is?
section: The prevalence of our anthropomophism thinking
text:
The prevalence of our anthropomophism thinking
The paper first shows how widespread this is in academic research. An analysis of over 250,000 research abstracts reveals a steady increase in human-like terminology. Words like “hallucinate,” “understand,” “learn,” and “achieve” are used to describe model behaviors. From a communication perspective, these are not neutral descriptors; they are framing devices that shape our expectations and might limit our thinking.

title: Being polite to AI is a form anthropomorphism — what else is?
text:
Five anthormorphstic assumptions we make


The Training Assumption: Believing human-like learning methods are optimal for models.


Limitation: Forcing a model to reason in step-by-step language (Chain-of-Thought) might be less effective than allowing it to reason in its own abstract “latent space”.
Alternative: Use byte-level tokenization (processing raw computer data) and explore reasoning methods that operate beyond the constraints of human language * **




The Alignment Assumption: Thinking models must reason about human values o be safe and helpful.


Limitation: Teaching models human values can lead to surface-level mimicry, misleading users into over-trusting or forming emotional attachments to systems that don’t actually understand values.
Alternative: Use control systems theory to treat alignment as an engineering problem of keeping a system’s output within specified bounds, rather than a moral one. * **




The Evaluation Assumption: Assuming model capabilities should be measured with human-like tests.


Limitation: Human benchmarks (like standardized tests) can be misleading and often fail to capture the unique ways AIs fail. Models can get good at passing these tests without real improvement in general capabilities.
Alternative: Design dynamic benchmarks and tests specifically tailored to AI failure modes, such as sensitivities to the probabilities in their training data. ***




The Behaviore Assumption: Attributing human-like intentions to a model’s behavior.


Limitation: Labeling a model’s output as “deceptive” or “sycophantic” incorrectly assigns a human illocutionary act (the speaker’s intent) to a system that has none. This can lead to flawed interventions that try to address the “motive” rather than the underlying technical cause.
Alternative: Reframe these behaviors as “role-play” or sophisticated simulation, where the model is simply reproducing linguistic patterns without any genuine internal state. 




The User Interaction Assumption: That interacting with an LLM should mirror human-to-human conversation.


Limitation: The standard chat interface encourages conversational habits that are often ineffective for getting high-quality outputs.This creates a “gulf of envisioning,” where users struggle to formulate prompts that leverage the system’s actual capabilities.
Alternative: Develop structured interaction frameworks and interfaces that more explicitly guide users and expose the system’s true functionality, rather than masking it behind a conversational layer. ***

title: Being polite to AI is a form anthropomorphism — what else is?
section: How does the user experience fit in?
text:
How does the user experience fit in?
It’s ironic that we just discussed how using polite, courteous language with LLMs might enhance performance or at least the user experience. This paper suggests that, for optimal technical performance, we might not use natural language to communicate with LLMs at all. This raises a fascinating question: Do we only need LLMs for instrumental tasks—to just get work done? Or is there also a need for phatic communication, the kind of social interaction that builds emotional bonds? This is especially important when considering diverse users, such as children, who may not have a sense of how the models function at all, leaving a potential for over-trust.
Perhaps the solution is a two-tiered approach. On a technical level, we should de-anthropomorphize AI to build more competent and reliable systems. The “human touch” can then be thoughtfully applied at the interface level through careful UX design, allowing us to consciously and ethically choose when and how to provide that sense of social support.

title: Personalized but excessively long suggestions from LLMs

title: Personalized but excessively long suggestions from LLMs
section: My LLMs sometimes know more about me than I do
text:
My LLMs sometimes know more about me than I do
It’s the beginning of another beautiful semester — and according to the syllabus of my communication course, we are required to pick a book from a list of seven on the topic of AI to read throughout the academic term.
Usually, I would let my large language model introduce each book to me to get a snapshot and then make a judgment myself. This time, I decided to take it a step further and treat the interaction as a small communicative experiment. I would ask the LLM to act as a consultant and actively suggest the best options for me.
This should be a reasonable task for an LLM: I’ve been using this particular model mainly for school and work since 2023, so our interaction history forms a rich data of my academic and intellectual interests. Therefore, it should be able to generate tailored suggestions. However,I decided to make my intention clear in the ask, because I don’t assume it will automatically take my background into account, which a human would probably do:




Image



Here, instead of merely paraphrasing the assignment, I included the full text from the syllabus. From a pragmatics perspective, this provides the LLM with maximum context for the current exchange (Shhh, not because I was too lazy).
After 42 seconds, the model returned a long response structured in a very deliberate way: * An opening comment on the assignment. * His top 3 picks with rationales.


 ***


A parting line, then a short introduction for each book.
Another parting line, then ideas for how the books could be incorporated into my existing work.



 ***


A final parting line, the suggested ranking list
Tips for the assignment and, finally, a follow-up question to invite more interaction.



 ***

The response was comprehensive, seemingly designed to anticipate and address all my potential questions.

title: Personalized but excessively long suggestions from LLMs
section: Is unnecessarily long for a natural human interaction
text:
Is unnecessarily long for a natural human interaction
While I found the response useful, it was excessively lengthy, especially considering the computational energy LLMs consume. I often have the sense that they favor exhaustiveness over the brevity we often value in human conversation, because talking is energy-consuming.

title: Personalized but excessively long suggestions from LLMs
section: But here are the things I truly appreciated:
text:
But here are the things I truly appreciated:

It provided a ready-to-use ranked list. The LLM correctly parsed the prompt’s explicit instructions (“rank your preferences”) and structured its primary output to meet that specific need.
It provided rationales connecting to my past work, which allowed me to critically evaluate the rationales and re-weigh my current prioritization.
It suggested practical applications. The ideas for incorporating the book’s content into my other projects were genuinely insightful.

Interestingly, this final point highlights a key difference between human and AI communication. It’s difficult to imagine a human expert spontaneously generating such a detailed list of potential operational connections of each book with my past experience in a casual conversation. The tips for class would also be cognitively exausive to provide. While the cognitive load requried for these content would be too high for a human talker, they are easy-peasy for a LLM.

title: Personalized but excessively long suggestions from LLMs
text:
Different mental manipulation mechanisms
So, although the tones and expressions look humane, GPT’s very ability to perform this low-cost, high-output analysis in a causal converstion is actually inhuman, or unatural. It doesn’t rely on the same mental shortcuts as human do. To him, generating these chunks of tasks have no different from the other chunks, computationally.
